# Red-Team: q\* = m·B_P/B_H Simultaneous-Finish Split

## Grounding the mechanic first

Operationalizing the terms: path P requires B_P work-units, path H requires B_H. You route throughputs x_P, x_H. With path efficiencies e_P, e_H, completion times are T_P = B_P/(x_P·e_P), T_H = B_H/(x_H·e_H). Setting T_P = T_H:

**x_P/x_H = (e_H/e_P)·(B_P/B_H) = m·B_P/B_H**, with m = e_H/e_P.

So q\* is a *throughput ratio*, and the formula silently assumes seven things: (i) linear returns to flow, (ii) B values are fixed and truthful, (iii) no cross-path conversion, (iv) enforcement binds per-agent, (v) exact arithmetic, (vi) completion is atomic, (vii) scoring is continuous in time. Every bypass below breaks one of these. Each mitigation is stated as a deterministic rule — same input state, same forced output, no discretion, no probability.

## The twelve bypass attempts and their fixes

**1. Stale-budget skew.** Mutate B_P or B_H after the split is locked in (donate, expand scope, trigger an event) so the running q\* was computed against numbers that no longer hold. P gets systematically overfed.
*Fix:* Commit-reveal snapshot. q\* binds to a `snapshot_id` taken at a fixed ledger tick. Any subsequent mutation spawns a new snapshot and **prorates in-flight allocation back to the old q\*** before switching. Recompute is forced, not optional.

**2. Cross-path laundering.** Convert H-stock into P-stock mid-run (crafting, trade recipes) so measured B diverges from true remaining need at the moment the split is applied.
*Fix:* Single total order on ledger events per tick; conversions book **before** the split computation. Define B_i(t) = remaining-unmet-requirement evaluated against post-conversion state each tick. Append-only ledger makes double-counting structurally impossible — there is no second ordering to exploit.

**3. Pre-window grinding.** Do all P-work before the split regime activates, so when q\* applies, P needs zero more and 100% of capacity floods H. The "balanced finish" is theater.
*Fix:* Account cumulatively from a world-set origin O, not from regime activation. Completion test: ∫₀^T x_P ≥ B_P,total with the integral starting at O. Additionally impose a hard ceiling on pre-origin credits (deterministic cap, e.g., 20% of B_P) so the origin cannot be trivially front-loaded either.

**4. Obligation burning.** Destroy or discard H-stock to shrink B_H, which *raises* q\* = m·B_P/B_H and overfeeds P; restore H later at leisure.
*Fix:* B_i is **obligation minus delivered receipts**, never current holdings. Waste decrements nothing. Obligations are written immutably at run-open; only validated delivery receipts decrement them. Burning stock costs the burner their own completion time and touches nobody else's ratio.

**5. Identity splitting across chairs.** If the split binds per-entity, run N accounts: assign the large-capacity one entirely to P, small ones to H. The global mix deviates from q\* even though every individual satisfies theirs.
*Fix:* Enforce on the **capacity-weighted aggregate**: Σ(x_i·w_i)/Σ(y_i·w_i) must satisfy q\*, where w_i is entity i's capacity share. Settlement check per epoch: |actual_mix − q\*| > ε ⇒ proportional clawback of the violating side's throughput credit. Sybil accounts don't help because weights, not headcount, enter the sum.

**6. Rounding-drift harvesting.** q\* is real; implementations quantize. Always round the constrained path down, sweep residue to the preferred path. Compounds over thousands of ticks into a material edge.
*Fix:* Exact rational arithmetic internally. Largest-remainder allocation per epoch with **mandatory carry-forward**: unallocated residue is tracked and must clear next epoch or auto-forfeits to whichever path is currently behind — never to player choice. Drift is bounded to one epoch's rounding unit, permanently.

**7. Rate-shift via upgrades.** Any buff, tool, or terrain effect changing e_P or e_H makes m stale; buy a P-rate boost mid-run and the old q\* now overfeeds H.
*Fix:* Recompute q\*_t every tick from current (B(t), r(t)): q\*_t = (e_H(t)/e_P(t))·(B_P(t)/B_H(t)). There is no cached m to abuse. (Alternative — freeze rates contractually at run-open — works but is weaker; continuous recompute dominates because staleness becomes impossible rather than penalized.)

**8. Premature-release race.** Claim a path complete at 99%, free its capacity to the other path, and let async verification catch up later.
*Fix:* Atomic ledger transition. Capacity frees **only** on a validated delivery receipt recorded in the same tick; completion is a state transition debiting the final requirement units synchronously. There is no window between "claimed" and "effective" because they are the same ledger write.

**9. Checkpoint desync.** If simultaneity is scored only at checkpoints, finish P at t−δ and H at exactly t. Both "finished together" at the checkpoint; P's unlock fired early.
*Fix:* Score is S = f(|T_P − T_H|), strictly decreasing, evaluated **continuously** from ledger timestamps — no checkpoint discretization exists to hide inside. Milestone payouts gate on a conjunction: both completion flags set within the same tick, atomically evaluated. δ > 0 loses value monotonically, so desyncing is never profitable even briefly.

**10. Input tampering.** If any term of q\* comes from a player-writable field, players simply write favorable B values.
*Fix:* Hard input whitelist: q\* reads only (a) genesis-immutable budget constants and (b) validated delivery receipt counters. Zero player-writable fields participate in the formula. Anyone can recompute q\* from public ledger state and verify the allocator's output bit-for-bit.

**11. Griefing injection.** A third party dumps junk obligations into your H path, inflating your denominator and wrecking your ratio.
*Fix:* Inbound transfers require recipient acceptance signature. Unsolicited deposits land in escrow and are **excluded from the ratio computation** until accepted. B_H counts only obligations the owner contracted; hostile inflation cannot reach the formula.

**12. Surplus-banking milestone rush.** If tiers pay on *cumulative* delivery, over-deliver to P early, bank the tiered rewards, then coast while H catches up to restore apparent balance.
*Fix:* Payouts key to the simultaneous-gate state (per fix 9's conjunction), not cumulative volume. Over-delivery past the current gate earns exactly zero incremental reward. The optimal strategy collapses to delivering precisely what keeps both gates opening together.

## What composes

Three load-bearing mechanisms collapse the whole list:

- **Ledger-truth computation** (fixes 1, 2, 10, 11): one append-only ledger, one total order, q\* computed only from committed state at tick boundaries. Kills every attack on inputs.
- **Exact continuous recompute** (fixes 6, 7): rationals, per-tick, no cached constants, mandatory carry. Kills every attack on staleness and precision.
- **Atomic conjunctive settlement** (fixes 8, 9, 12): completion, capacity release, and payout are a single state transition gated on both-paths-in-the-same-tick, scored continuously in |T_P − T_H|. Kills every attack on timing.

Fixes 3, 4, 5 stand alone as accounting rules (origin-anchored integrals, receipt-decremented obligations, capacity-weighted aggregates) but slot cleanly into the same ledger substrate. Implement those three mechanisms and the residual exploit surface is empty: every bypass reduces to mutating an input the formula no longer reads, or desynchronizing an outcome the scorer no longer tolerates.
reasoning:
The user is asking about a game world concept called "Ledger of Empty Chairs" — this appears to be a fictional or custom game design problem. They're asking me to red-team a mechanic: a measured split ratio q* = m·B_P/B_H that makes two resource paths finish together. I need to:

1. Understand what the mechanic is
2. Enumerate bypass attempts (ways players can exploit/circumvent it)
3. Give deterministic mitigations for each

Let me reason from first principles since "Ledger of Empty Chairs" isn't a known published game — I should treat it as a designed system and ground my analysis in the math of the formula itself.

**Understanding the mechanic:**

q* = m · B_P / B_H

- B_P and B_H are presumably two resource budgets/stockpiles — maybe "Bench/Pantry" vs "Hall"? Or Player-side budget vs House-side? In a "Ledger of Empty Chairs" theme, chairs could be seats/positions, resources could be labor/materials. Let's say:
  - B_P = budget for path P (e.g., "Provisions")
  - B_H = budget for path H (e.g., "Hearth")
  - m = some constant multiplier (a tuning parameter)
  - q* = the split fraction allocated to one path so both finish simultaneously.

The core idea: two resource paths with different total requirements (B_P, B_H) and possibly different rates; you split your throughput q between them such that completion times equalize. The classic simultaneous-finish condition:

If path i requires B_i work at rate r_i when fed fraction q_i of your total capacity C, then time T_i = B_i / (r_i · q_i). Setting T_P = T_H gives q_P/q_H = (B_P/r_P)/(B_H/r_H), normalized. So q* = m·B_P/B_H where m = r_H/r_P absorbs rate constants.

So the design intent: force balanced allocation; prevent dumping everything into the fast path. The measured split makes both finish together, presumably to prevent snowballing or hoarding.

**Red-teaming: enumerate bypass attempts.**

A bypass attempt = any player action or emergent behavior that lets a player get an advantage despite the enforced split — e.g., finishing one path early anyway, converting resources across paths, gaming the measurement of B_P/B_H, exploiting timing granularity, etc.

Let me enumerate systematically by attack surface:

1. **Budget inflation/deflation attacks (manipulate B_P or B_H):**
   - Since q* depends on B_P/B_H, if a player can change the denominators after committing the split, they skew it.
   - Attack: inflate B_H (or shrink B_P) right before/at measurement lock-in → q* computed on stale values → over-allocation to P finishes P early.
   - Deterministic mitigation: snapshot-and-freeze. Compute q* from budgets frozen at a fixed ledger tick (commit-reveal or two-phase commit); any post-snapshot mutation invalidates and recomputes. Deterministic rule: q* is bound to (snapshot_id); mutations create new snapshot with re-derived q*, and in-flight allocations are prorated back.

2. **Cross-path conversion / laundering:**
   - Convert H-resources into P-resources (crafting/trading) so the effective B_P shrinks while B_H grows, then the formula overfeeds P relative to true need... wait, actually if you convert, B_P drops, so q* = m·B_P/B_H drops, feeding P less — but you've already got stockpiled P. The exploit: convert during the run, so measured B at split-time ≠ actual remaining requirement.
   - Deterministic mitigation: define B_i as *remaining unmet requirement* evaluated each tick against current stockpiles + committed conversions; conversions are booked into the same ledger before the split computation, single ordering (total order on ledger events per tick). No double-counting because the ledger is append-only and deterministic order.

3. **Timing/race exploits (finish early via burst outside measured window):**
   - Attack: do all P-work before the split regime starts (pre-phase grinding), so when q* applies, P needs zero more, freeing 100% to H.
   - Mitigation: the split governs cumulative totals from a fixed origin, not marginal flows. Deterministic rule: completion condition defined as T where ∫q_P ≥ B_P_total from origin O; pre-O work counts toward B but the origin is set by world event, not player choice. Alternatively: cap pre-regime accrual (hard ceiling on B usable).

4. **Idle/burn attacks (waste to shift ratios):**
   - Deliberately burn H-resources to lower B_H → raises q* → more feed to P... wait q* = m·B_P/B_H; lowering B_H raises q*. If q* is the share to P, burning H inflates P's share. Then later restore H cheaply. Net: P finished early.
   - Deterministic mitigation: burned/wasted resources still count toward B_H until replaced — i.e., B_H = original commitment minus only *delivered* progress, not current holdings. Waste doesn't reduce obligation. Ledger records obligations immutably; only delivery receipts decrement.

5. **Multiple identities / chair-splitting (the "empty chairs" flavor suggests seats/players):**
   - Run parallel accounts each with their own q*, aggregate throughput to one path. If the split is per-entity, N entities give you N independent splits; you allocate each entity fully to one path and combine.
   - Wait — if each entity must split its own throughput, combining entities still forces the global ratio to be the weighted average of individual q*s; you can't beat the average unless entities differ in capacity. If capacities differ (entity A big, entity B small), put the big one on P and small on H — the global mix deviates from q*.
   - Deterministic mitigation: enforce the constraint on aggregate throughput per *chair* (seat) rather than per actor, or normalize: weight each actor's contribution by capacity so Σ contributions satisfy the global ratio; deterministic check at settlement: |actual_mix − q*| > ε ⇒ clawback proportional to violation.

6. **Rounding/granularity exploitation:**
   - q* is real-valued; implementation quantizes (integer units, discrete ticks). Rounding residue accumulates: always round down the constrained path, dump residue to preferred path. Over many ticks, drift compounds.
   - Deterministic mitigation: exact rational arithmetic with a deterministic remainder-carry ledger (like largest-remainder method per epoch, carry-forward). Residue is tracked and must be spent within the next epoch or forfeits — never silently rounds in the exploiter's favor.

7. **Rate manipulation (m is not truly constant):**
   - m encodes relative rates r_H/r_P. If any upgrade/tool/temporary buff changes r_P, the true balance point moves; a player buys rate boosts mid-run on one path only.
   - Deterministic mitigation: recompute q* every tick from current rates: q*_t = (B_P(t)/r_P(t)) normalization; or freeze rates for the duration once the run opens (rate locks are part of the commitment). Pick one: continuous recompute kills the exploit deterministically because there's no stale m to abuse.

8. **Partial-completion claim / verification lag:**
   - Claim a path is done when it's 99% done; the freed capacity goes to the other path before audit catches up. Async verification gap.
   - Deterministic mitigation: synchronous settlement per tick; no capacity is freed until a delivery receipt is validated in-ledger. Completion is a ledger state transition, atomic with the resource debit.

9. **Deadline/schedule gaming (when does "finish together" get checked?):**
   - If the simultaneity is only scored at a checkpoint T_check, a player can front-load P to finish slightly before T_check and H exactly at T_check — both "finish together" at the checkpoint but P was actually finished earlier, giving earlier access to whatever P unlocks.
   - Deterministic mitigation: reward is continuous in max(T_P,T_H) minus min(T_P,T_H) — i.e., payoff strictly decreasing in |T_P − T_H|, evaluated continuously, not at checkpoints. Any asymmetry is immediately penalized, so no incentive to desynchronize even briefly.

10. **Oracle/measurement tampering (who measures B?):**
    - If B_P/B_H are reported by players (self-reporting ledger entries), lie about them.
    - Deterministic mitigation: budgets are world-authored constants written at genesis of the run into an immutable ledger entry; no player-writable field participates in q*. All inputs to q* are either constants or derived from validated deliveries.

11. **Overflow/deadlock griefing (negative play):**
    - Not a gain-seeking bypass but a sabotage: another player dumps garbage into your H path to inflate B_H, distorting your q*.
    - Deterministic mitigation: B_H counts only obligations contracted by the owner; inbound transfers require recipient acceptance signature; unsolicited deposits are escrowed and excluded from the ratio computation.

12. **Speculative over-delivery / banking ahead:**
    - Deliver more than needed to one path early, bank surplus, then the formula sees reduced remaining B and starves that path — but the surplus already secured its milestone rewards.
    - Actually this is legitimate-ish; the exploit version is if milestones pay out on cumulative delivery, over-delivering to grab tiered rewards early then letting the other path catch up. 
    - Deterministic mitigation: milestone payouts keyed to *simultaneous* completion state (both paths' gates open in same tick), not cumulative delivery. Payout function is a conjunction, atomically evaluated.

Now let me also nail the math of the base case so the answer is grounded:

Setup: Total capacity C per tick. Path P needs B_P units, path H needs B_H. Feeding fraction q to P gives rate q·C (assuming unit efficiency, or fold efficiencies into m: effective rate to P = q·C·e_P, to H = (1−q)·C·e_H).

T_P = B_P/(q·C·e_P), T_H = B_H/((1−q)·C·e_H).
Set equal: B_P/(q e_P) = B_H/((1−q) e_H)
⇒ B_P(1−q)e_H = B_H q e_P
⇒ B_P e_H − B_P e_H q = B_H e_P q
⇒ q(B_H e_P + B_P e_H) = B_P e_H
⇒ q* = (B_P e_H)/(B_H e_P + B_P e_H).

Hmm, the given form is q* = m·B_P/B_H. That matches if we define q as a *ratio* q = (feed to P)/(feed to H) rather than a fraction of total. Let's check: let x = amount to P, y = amount to H, ratio q = x/y.
T_P = B_P/(x e_P), T_H = B_H/(y e_H).
Equal ⇒ B_P y e_H = B_H x e_P ⇒ x/y = (B_P e_H)/(B_H e_P) = (e_H/e_P)(B_P/B_H) = m·B_P/B_H with m = e_H/e_P. 

So q* = m·B_P/B_H is the *ratio of throughputs* (not shares) needed, with m absorbing relative efficiencies. Good — that's the grounded reading. I'll state this interpretation explicitly since the problem says "measured split," which fits ratio-of-flows.

Key invariant: the formula assumes linearity (constant returns to flow) and additive, non-interactive paths. Every bypass above is essentially attacking one hidden assumption:
- Linearity (rate manipulation #7)
- Additivity/no cross-conversion (#2)
- Fixed budgets (#1, #4, #9-grief #11)
- Per-agent enforcement (#5)
- Exact arithmetic (#6)
- Atomic completion semantics (#8, #12)
- Trusted inputs (#10)

That gives me a clean taxonomy for presentation. Let me structure the answer:

1. Ground the model (what q* means, what assumptions it silently makes).
2. Table/list of bypasses grouped by the assumption they break, each with concrete attack mechanics and a deterministic mitigation (stated as an implementable rule, not a vibe).
3. Maybe close with the meta-mitigation: continuous recomputation from ledger truth + strict penalty continuity, which collapses several attack classes at once.

Deterministic mitigation means: a fixed rule that produces the same outcome every time, no discretion, no probabilistic detection. So each mitigation should be stated as: input condition → forced output action, computable by anyone from ledger state.

Format thoughts: This deserves a fairly thorough response — the user asked to "enumerate" and be "concrete, exact." A numbered list of bypasses with (attack, why it works, deterministic fix) structure. Use headers sparingly, keep each item tight. Math inline where needed. Probably 900–1400 words. Markdown lists are appropriate here since it's a technical enumeration. Avoid tables maybe — or use one compact table for the assumption→attack map. Actually a short grounding section with the derivation, then ~10 enumerated bypasses each with Attack/Mechanism/Deterministic fix lines, then a brief closing note on which mitigations compose. Keep fluff out.

Let me finalize the list, trimming overlaps. Final enumeration:

0. Model grounding: q* = m·B_P/B_H is the throughput ratio x_P/x_H equalizing T_P=T_H under linear returns; m = e_H/e_P. Assumptions: (i) linear rates, (ii) B's are fixed and truthful, (iii) no cross-path conversion, (iv) enforcement per-agent, (v) exact arithmetic, (vi) completion is atomic, (vii) scoring continuous.

Bypasses:
1. Stale-budget skew (mutate B after lock-in) → snapshot & recompute binding.
2. Cross-path laundering (convert H→P mid-run) → single total-order ledger; B_i = remaining-unmet computed post-conversion each tick.
3. Pre-window grinding (do P work before split regime) → cumulative-from-origin accounting with world-set origin; hard ceiling on pre-origin credits.
4. Obligation burning (destroy H stock to raise q*) → B = obligation minus delivered receipts, holdings irrelevant; waste decrements nothing.
5. Capacity-weighted identity splitting (multi-account) → enforce on aggregate capacity-weighted mix; settlement check |mix − q*| ≤ ε with proportional clawback.
6. Rounding-drift harvesting → exact rationals, largest-remainder with mandatory carry-forward per epoch; unspent residue forfeits to the constrained path automatically (never to the player's choice).
7. Rate-shifting via upgrades (m goes stale) → recompute q*_t each tick from current (B,r); or contractually freeze rates at run open. Continuous recompute is strictly safer; pick it.
8. Premature completion claims / async gap → atomic ledger transition: capacity frees only on validated receipt in the same tick; no optimistic release.
9. Checkpoint desync (finish early but inside checkpoint tolerance) → score = f(|T_P − T_H|) strictly decreasing, evaluated continuously; payout gated on conjunction of both completions in same tick.
10. Self-reported inputs → q* reads only genesis-immutable constants and validated delivery receipts; no player-writable field in the formula.
11. Griefing injection (third party inflates your B_H) → inbound transfers require acceptance signature; unsolicited deposits escrowed, excluded from ratio.
12. Surplus-banking milestone rush → payouts keyed to simultaneous-gate state (conjunction), not cumulative volume; over-delivery earns nothing extra.

Maybe merge 8 into 12 partially... they're distinct enough: 8 is about capacity release timing, 12 about reward timing. Keep both but keep each tight.

Also worth noting the composition: mitigations 1+2+10 all reduce to "one append-only ledger, total order, q* computed only from committed state at tick boundary" — a single architectural fix kills three classes. And 7+6 reduce to "recompute exactly, every tick, in rationals." And 8+9+12 reduce to "atomic, conjunctive, continuous settlement." So the closing can group into three load-bearing mechanisms: (A) ledger-truth computation, (B) exact continuous recompute, (C) atomic conjunctive settlement.

Length check: 12 items × ~60–80 words each plus grounding and closing ≈ 1100–1300 words. That fits "thorough, concrete" without bloat. Headers: minimal — maybe bold lead-ins per item instead of full headers, with a short intro and a short synthesis. Numbered list format.
